blocks.text: Babylon was the Neo-Babylonian imperial capital and received deported Judeans after campaigns against Jerusalem. It was not merely a symbol but a major political, religious, economic, and scribal center where displaced communities lived. The city later passed to Cyrus in 539 BCE, yet Judean communities remained in Babylonia into the Persian period. The psalm’s setting therefore reflects an enduring life in dispersion, not simply a brief interruption before everyone returned.

sections.title: A Place of Displacement and Imperial Power

blocks.text: Biblical texts portray Babylon in two connected ways: as the concrete place where displaced Judeans built lives and as an imperial power held accountable to God. That tension helps explain why Psalm 137 can remember ordinary existence beside Babylon’s rivers while expressing grief, protest, and fierce loyalty to Jerusalem. Babylonian records come from different institutions and social settings, so no single kind of document describes the whole experience of the city or its deported communities.

One debated approach reads Psalm 137 within a wider pattern in the Psalter: communal psalms preserve memories of sanctuary destruction and Babylonian exile, while Book V also gathers thanksgiving for return, festival praise, meditation on Torah, and Songs of Ascents oriented toward worship. On this reading, the book preserves unresolved exile grief alongside material concerned with restoration and renewed worship.
